title: The Nature of Opportunity and the Fullness of Sin
english: He works the corruption of the earth. For this made men blameless, if the inability to be adorned toward God worked a sorrow; but the hardship of ways is shown through the corruption of the earth, just as it was foretold, of men corrupting the way of God, which had taken hold to prosper toward blessedness. Such are those having heard the words of Jesus and not doing them.

And if it also shows the flesh of man, as is often said, one should observe whether 'all flesh corrupted his way' (Ps 145:17) shows how each man has strayed from his own opinion. But that flesh is said instead of man is clear from 'I will pour out from my spirit upon all flesh' (Isa 44:3), and 'He will judge all flesh' (Isa 40:6). Therefore all those of the generation of Noah, having become earthly and fleshy, each strayed from 'his way' (Gen 6:11) which he had received; for the way is called to be received of him and to be given to God. Thus they corrupted their own way or the way of God; for both are possible.

And God said to Noah: 'The time of every man comes against me, because the earth was filled with injustice from them' (Gen 6:11). Many of the written things have a more useful history for the many. For these, living by sensation and glory, do not reach the truly great and profitable things. And let the said thing be upon an example.

Jesus healed a blind man from birth, and Lazarus, having had four days in the tomb, he brought out by command alone, and again the one in the cave, remaining in much decay, he raised. These things were for the sensible fulfillment and were symbolic: the one [healing] the blind from birth showing the sight of a soul that had never seen, because it had been overturned in sin and ignorance from soft nails, and again the one already pathless and having lost hope, having fallen from the blessed life, was shown symbolically coming back to it through Jesus, and the one seized by decay, then having been saved, testified to the return of a soul falling into insensibility. But these are more wonderful and greater than the healing of bodies, since the essence of the soul is more precious than the body, but which the many do not know. He, therefore, explaining the paradoxes thus to them, makes it more useful, and in the things now set forth of the history...

It also has a more useful benefit for the many. For what does he say? 'The opportunity for every man has come upon the earth' (Luke 19:44). And Peter also says that by the patience of God the deluge was delayed, so that repentance might be given.

For it has been revealed that the construction of the ark took place in a hundred years, so that seeing men and inquiring about the cause might take the opportunity for repentance. But opportunity here must not be thought of as being called by someone a time-keeper; for not fate holds sway over things, but everything happens by the will of God.

Therefore, it should be understood that 'the opportunity for every man has come upon the earth' means the almost-fullness of the sinning men, by which the bringing on of vengeance must be approached, as it is said: 'For the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet full unto this time' (Gen 15:16), instead of saying 'they have not sinned so much that their repentance be known.' For God does not bring wrath upon every single day, even though sins are being committed; rather, He does this by providing a place for repentance and giving the opportunity to recognize their own sinning; but when thus the things concerning them are completed so that they no longer have opportunity to recognize [their sin], the time has come for them to suffer.

And once the mention of the filling up of sin has occurred, this is to be noted: that it is not the same to fill up sins in one man and in a whole nation. For among the many, all sins are found to be present, such as one being unmanageable and another being spared, one being bold and another cowardly, and again one being licentious and another being foolish; but for one man, it is impossible to find these opposing vices in excess and deficiency. For it is possible for all virtues to be in a man, for they follow one another, but the vices are not so, because of the things previously mentioned.

And these things being a digression, let us return to the beginning: 'The opportunity for every man has come.' No one has such sins that they might be forgiven him; and just as an excellent physician, even if it happens at night, sets a time for the sick to receive nourishment according to the state of the disease, so also is the present thing being said. For when men have reached the extremity of sin, through which the deluge is brought, this happens.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Divine Will and the Ark
english: They act without being recognized. It is not necessary to suppose it is a lie that the time of every man has come, even if eight were saved in the ark; for here the general has been taken instead of 'for the most part'.

If, however, the 'every man' says, 'For where are strife and jealousy among you, are you not men?' (James 3:16), Noah is not subject to this by surpassing the human condition; and thus it is true that the time of every man has come, according to that which is called to sin in this way. Nor is 'against me' added in vain; for no mortal possesses the knowing of the time, by which one might have worthily acted so that the rest might have been made known. For this indeed no mortal truly knows; for if he were knowing the hearts, he would not even have helped by quickly turning back those who had come into sin.

For the only thing belonging to the unexceedable goodness, the goodness of essence which is not diminished, is to see the hidden and to know the time. If even someone of mortals participates in goodness from God by disposition, yet he is ignorant of the impositions of sins and the causes, just as God, knowing all, knows the time of the reprimand, therefore it is said 'against me' and 'because the earth was filled with injustice from them'. It is fitting that this too is said; for punishment does not come upon them because of the sins of others. It is also evident from this that such a death did not come upon them by fate; for since he says 'the earth was filled with injustice from them', the time has come, which would not have been established, unless they were sinning.

Yes, and behold, 'I will destroy them and the earth' (Jonah 3:4). The philanthropy and goodness of God are shown through these by foretelling what is to come, so that by the fear of what is expected, he might restrain the evil, which also happened to the Ninevites upon hearing the prophet Jonah: 'In three days Nineveh shall be overthrown' (Jonah 3:4). Consequently, too, to the righteous man he foretells these things and pre-arranges the making of the ark, putting forward this construction more clearly for the sake of every proclamation toward repentance, and he promises to destroy them and the earth, since it was necessary for this. For there are many reprimands given by God for the sake of the recognition of sins occurring; he wants...

For he says that he wished to gather all men into the knowledge of truth, as a bird gathers its young under its wings, but you did not wish to (Matt 23:37). For necessity does not force the good to become so, nor is it possible; for such a thing is no longer good. But when God, knowing all things, after many admonitions finds those whom he admonishes not obeying, he destroys them, according to what is profitable for his judgment. And the earth is also destroyed—that is, the things in the earth—for this is what 'the earth' signifies appropriately; for the things of men perishing, it was necessary for the things standing through them to pass away also. Just as the birds were left behind through Noah and those with him, and likewise the birds of all other animals were left behind.

Make for yourself an ark of squared timber; you shall make an ark for the sick; and you shall make it secure inside and outside with pitch (Gen 6:14). And so you shall make the ark: three hundred cubits the length of the ark, and fifty cubits the breadth, and thirty cubits its height. You shall make the ark by gathering [pieces] together, and you shall complete it one cubit by one cubit upward; and you shall make the door of the ark on the side. Make for it two or three decks. And I, behold, I bring the flood upon the earth, to destroy all flesh, in which is the spirit of life under heaven; and whatever is on the earth shall perish (Gen 6:17).

The phrase 'of squared timber' has the greater following, being commanded to make Noah's ark, first so that much time would not be consumed in dividing them, and secondly, which is more truthful, so that being made from whole timbers it might be more secure; for it was going to encounter storms and not a small gale, against which it would not have withstood if it had not been constructed from whole timbers. And 'the sick' is also useful, which are divided places, because of these two things: first, so that the habitation of the animals, which he was going to bring with him, would not be mixed, and second, for the joining of the construction; [it is] weaker...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Utility of Divine Words vs. Idle Speech
english: For it was—if fifty in width, three hundred in length, and thirty cubits in height—existing as an unconnected thing. It was well-sealed both outside and inside to prevent water from entering toward nothingness.

And indeed, the fact that the length was greater than the width was good; for in this way it was easy to move, since even the boats are in proportion to this shape. And if someone were to say that it became square underneath, this is not without truth; for it was made not for sailing previously, but for guarding, and for this reason it became so; otherwise it would have been quickly worn down, if it were not square. And it was joined together appropriately, so that the influx of the waters might have a sliding effect and not, as if against rock, throw the waves upward everywhere by its height. And the making of the door on the sides was appropriately arranged.

The dwellings were constructed appropriately so as to endure all the animals being brought in, both those and those for food. And the passage, 'But I, even I, bring a flood upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life under heaven; whatever is on the earth shall perish' (Genesis 6:17), is indeed awakening, as previously stated, and shows that both those on the earth and those in the air shall perish; for perhaps the aquatic ones were saved. And 'I establish my covenant with you' (Genesis 9:9). The covenant made by God with Noah does not appear to be an alliance, as Symmachus and Aquila interpreted. Perhaps so that He might not despise the words, the future was revealed to Noah, so that he might be hopeful concerning the things to come and might instruct, and his own generation, as 'God brought these things upon them because of sins; and you are being saved through righteousness' (Genesis 6:13), so that the shame of wickedness might be shown and the attraction of virtue; not as virtue exists as a pleasant wage, but because the diligent one, not being subject to the manner of punishment, does not rest from it. And 'I establish' shows the stability here. If you, your sons, your wife, and the wives of your sons enter into the ark (Genesis 7:7). The Savior in the Gospel said—

Regarding every idle word, men will give an account on the day of judgment; but an idle word is useless and having nothing beneficial. If this is not presented as a burden to men, much more do the divine words not contain such a thing, but everything is brought forth usefully in them, and we have seen this from the things set forth.

When entering the ark, Noah arranged the sons, and to the wife the wives of his sons; and when the time for going out into the earth remained, the flooding having ceased, the saying is noted thus: 'And God said to Noah: You and your wife and your sons and the wives of your sons come out of the ark' (Gen 7:7). For it was proper, since the corruption of men was about to happen, that the righteous should not be without companions, so as to use the married ones. Therefore he separated the wives of the men, saying: 'Let in you and your sons and your wife and the wives of your sons' (Gen 8:18); but when it was received that the succession was about to be restored again, he gave to Noah the wife, saying: 'Come out, you and your wife and your sons and the wives of your sons' (Gen 8:18).

And that because of custom it was not spoken appropriately, but with observation, it is possible to say, and to believe the Gospel, it having been said by the Savior: 'No one is able to serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other; you cannot serve God and mammon' (Matt 6:24). And it is clear that the love of money is the slavery of mammon, and [it is] upon every evil. For it is in no way possible to serve both evil and virtue; for the one doing sin is a slave of sin, and everyone who does [sin] hates the evil things. For those who love [God] hate the evil things. 'For either he will hate the one and love the other'—for the virtuous one loves God and hates evil—'or he will hold to the one and despise the other,' which is precisely said; for he said 'to hold against' the evil, not 'to love' it.
